title: “WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED”—WHAT IF WE’VE BEEN USING JESUS’ WORDS TO MEAN SOMETHING HE WASN’T TALKING ABOUT?
paragraphs: “WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED”—WHAT IF WE’VE BEEN USING JESUS’ WORDS TO MEAN SOMETHING HE WASN’T TALKING ABOUT?

One of Christianity’s most comforting Bible verses is also one of its most misunderstood. And when you discover what Jesus was actually saying, you may never look at church, forgiveness, broken relationships, or the presence of Christ the same way again.
There is something almost every Christian has heard.
Maybe you heard it in a Wednesday night prayer meeting when only four people showed up.
Maybe it was during a Bible study in somebody’s living room, when the pastor looked around at the empty chairs and tried to encourage the few who came.
Or maybe you heard it during one of those seasons when your church attendance was shrinking, your ministry was struggling, and you were quietly wondering whether God was still moving.
Someone smiled and said:
“Don’t worry. The Bible says, ‘Where two or three are gathered in My name, there am I among them.’”
And everyone felt better.
Because surely, if even two people show up, Jesus promises to be there.
Right?
Well…
What if I told you that Jesus really did say those words, but He was addressing something far more uncomfortable than a poorly attended prayer meeting?

What if the verse we use to comfort ourselves about empty chairs was originally spoken in a conversation about sin, confrontation, witnesses, repentance, forgiveness, and the terrifying responsibility of the church to handle broken relationships faithfully?
And what if understanding that context would not take away the comfort of the verse…
…but reveal a deeper kind of comfort?
The kind that meets us when relationships collapse.
When someone sins against us.
When we are the ones who have sinned.
When pride makes reconciliation almost impossible.
When the truth must be spoken, even though everybody would rather stay silent.
Stay with me, because the words immediately surrounding Matthew 18:20 may change the way you understand what it means for Jesus to be present among His people.
And the most surprising part?
The passage that begins with a lost sheep eventually leads us to a Savior who refuses to treat reconciliation as something optional.
Jesus was not merely talking about how many people attend a gathering.
He was teaching His disciples how to live together under His authority when sin threatens to tear them apart.
And that changes everything.
“For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”
— Matthew 18:20, King James Version
Beautiful words.
True words.
But here is the question we rarely ask:
Why did Jesus say them?
Because a Bible verse can be quoted accurately and still be applied carelessly.
We can repeat the exact words of Jesus while missing the very thing Jesus was teaching.
And sometimes, the most dangerous misunderstandings are not the ones that sound obviously false.
They are the ones that sound so familiar that nobody thinks to open the Bible and read the surrounding verses.
Go back with me to Matthew 18.
Not just verse 20.
Start where the conversation begins to unfold.
Jesus is teaching His disciples about humility, the seriousness of causing others to stumble, and the Father's concern for those who wander.
He speaks of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to seek the one that has gone astray.
Then, in Matthew 18:14, He says:
“Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.”
Notice the heart of God.
He does not delight in losing people.
He cares about those who wander.
And immediately after this, Jesus turns toward something that can destroy fellowship among believers.
Sin.
Not the kind we discuss safely from a distance.
The kind that happens between people who know each other.
People who worship together.
People who call one another brother and sister.
People who once trusted each other.
People who now avoid eye contact across the sanctuary.
Jesus says in Matthew 18:15:
“Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.”
Read that final phrase again.
“Thou hast gained thy brother.”
Not, “You have won the argument.”
Not, “You have exposed the sinner.”
Not, “You have proven that you were right.”
You have gained your brother.
The objective is restoration.
Truth matters. Sin matters. Accountability matters.
But Jesus does not teach confrontation as a weapon for humiliating someone.
He teaches a process in which love refuses to pretend that sin is harmless, while seeking to recover the person who has gone astray.
Think about how different that is from the way we often handle conflict.
Someone hurts us.
Instead of speaking to them, we tell five other people.
We share carefully edited versions of the story.
We collect sympathizers.
We post vague messages online about betrayal, loyalty, and fake Christians.
We pray that God will expose them.
But sometimes, if we are willing to be painfully honest, we are not praying for restoration.
We are praying for vindication.
We want people to know we were right.
We want the person who hurt us to feel what we felt.
And somewhere along the way, the brother or sister we were supposed to seek becomes the enemy we are determined to defeat.
Jesus confronts that impulse.
He tells us to begin privately.

That does not mean every situation is safe for a private confrontation. Abuse, violence, coercion, and criminal wrongdoing may require immediate protection, appropriate authorities, and outside help. Jesus' instruction must never be used to force a victim into an unsafe meeting or to conceal a crime.
But in ordinary interpersonal offenses, the principle is unmistakable.
Do not turn a person's failure into public entertainment when a truthful, loving conversation may yet restore the relationship.
And if the person refuses to listen?
Jesus continues.
“But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.”
— Matthew 18:16, KJV
There it is.
Two or three.
Does that sound familiar?
It should.
Because the phrase in Matthew 18:20 does not suddenly appear out of nowhere.
Jesus has already introduced the importance of two or three witnesses.
And He is drawing on a much older biblical principle.
Deuteronomy 19:15 says:
“At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.”
This is not about creating a spiritual atmosphere through attendance numbers.
It is about establishing a matter responsibly.
It is about truth being examined rather than accusations being accepted carelessly.
It is about refusing to let one person's untested claim automatically become the judgment of an entire community.
In the Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 19:15, we find:
עַל־פִּי שְׁנֵי עֵדִים אוֹ עַל־פִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה עֵדִים יָקוּם דָּבָר
‘Al-pi shenei ‘edim o ‘al-pi sheloshah ‘edim yaqum davar.
Literally, in sense:
“By the testimony of two witnesses or by the testimony of three witnesses, a matter shall be established.”
The Hebrew word עֵדִים (‘edim) means “witnesses.”
And יָקוּם דָּבָר (yaqum davar) conveys the establishment or confirmation of a matter.
The context is judicial.
It concerns responsible testimony and the protection of justice.
Now return to Matthew 18.
Jesus is not inventing a magical numerical formula.
He is speaking within a biblical framework of witnesses, accountability, and communal responsibility.
If a brother refuses private correction, one or two others become involved.
If the matter remains unresolved, Jesus describes bringing it before the church.
And if there is persistent refusal even to listen to the church, He describes a serious change in how the community relates to the unrepentant person.
These are weighty instructions.
They require humility, careful examination of facts, impartiality, patience, and obedience to Christ.
They are not permission for church leaders to become dictators.
They are not permission to punish someone for asking legitimate questions.
They are not permission to silence people who report abuse.
They are certainly not permission to call every disagreement “rebellion.”
A church exercising discipline must itself remain accountable to Scripture.
Because the authority belongs to Jesus.
Not to the pastor's ego.
Not to a religious institution's reputation.
Not to the loudest person in the room.
And then Jesus says something extraordinary.
“Verily I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever ye shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”
— Matthew 18:18, KJV
Those words are sometimes treated as if Christians can simply declare whatever they want and compel heaven to approve.
But in this context, Jesus is speaking about the church's serious responsibility to make judgments under His authority.
The Greek wording is especially worth examining.
Matthew 18:18 contains the expressions:
ἔσται δεδεμένα ἐν οὐρανῷ
estai dedemena en ouranō
And:
ἔσται λελυμένα ἐν οὐρανῷ
estai lelymena en ouranō
These constructions combine a future form of “to be” with perfect passive participles.
They can be represented quite literally as “will have been bound in heaven” and “will have been loosed in heaven.”
Scholars discuss how best to express the force of these constructions in English, and we should not pretend that one grammatical observation settles every theological question.
But this much is clear from the passage: Jesus is not handing the church an independent power to make heaven obey human wishes.
The church is accountable to the authority of heaven.
Its judgments must be faithful to the will and teaching of Christ.
Imagine how differently Christians would approach conflict if we remembered that.
Imagine a pastor who trembles before God more than he worries about protecting his position.
Imagine church members who seek truth instead of gossip.
Imagine leaders who care more about restoring a wounded believer than defending the institution's image.
Imagine a sinner who is corrected without being treated as disposable.
Imagine a wounded person whose testimony is taken seriously instead of being dismissed for the sake of appearances.
This is not weakness.
This is what it looks like when the people of Jesus submit to the Lordship of Jesus.
And now we reach the verse immediately before the famous promise.
“Again I say unto you, That if two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven.”
— Matthew 18:19, KJV
We often quote this verse as a universal guarantee that whenever two Christians agree about something in prayer, God must grant the request.
But that interpretation creates serious problems.
What if two Christians agree to pray for something selfish?
What if their request contradicts God's revealed will?
What if two sincere believers agree that a sick loved one should recover, but that person dies?
Does that mean they did not have enough faith?
Does it mean Jesus failed to keep His promise?
No.
Scripture does not teach that agreement between believers overrides the wisdom and will of God.
First John 5:14 explicitly connects confidence in prayer with asking according to God's will.
And Matthew 18:19 must be read in the context of the discussion that surrounds it.
The Greek word translated “agree” is:
συμφωνήσωσιν (symphōnēsōsin)
It comes from συμφωνέω (symphōneō), meaning “to agree” or “to be in accord.”
It is related to the word from which English gets “symphony.”
That connection is memorable, but we must be careful not to build a doctrine on the modern musical associations of an ancient word.
The point is agreement.
And in this passage, agreement is being discussed in the setting of the church's response to sin and the exercise of its responsibilities before God.
The immediate context strongly favors understanding this promise in connection with that serious communal work, rather than as a blank check for any two people who make the same request.
Then comes the statement we have heard all our lives.
Matthew 18:20.
In the Greek New Testament:
οὗ γάρ εἰσιν δύο ἢ τρεῖς συνηγμένοι εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα, ἐκεῖ εἰμι ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν.
Hou gar eisin dyo ē treis synēgmenoi eis to emon onoma, ekei eimi en mesō autōn.
A close English rendering is:
“For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am among them.”
Notice the little word γάρ (gar).
It means “for” or “because.”
That word matters.
Jesus is connecting His promise to what He has just said.
He is giving a reason for the assurance surrounding the gathering and agreement of His disciples.
The phrase συνηγμένοι (synēgmenoi) refers to people who have been gathered together.
And εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα (eis to emon onoma) means “in my name,” carrying the significance of gathering in relation to Jesus' name and authority.
It does not mean merely mentioning Jesus at the beginning of a meeting.
It does not mean putting a Christian label on an activity.
To gather in His name is to gather as people who belong to Him and are accountable to Him.
And ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν (en mesō autōn) means “among them” or “in their midst.”
Now hear the promise again.
Where two or three are gathered in His name, Jesus is among them.
In its immediate context, this is a breathtaking assurance that Christ is not absent when His people faithfully carry out the difficult responsibilities He has given them.
He is not indifferent when the church must confront sin.
He is not uninvolved when truth and reconciliation are at stake.
His people are not left to exercise these responsibilities as though they were merely a human organization.
They act under the authority of the risen Lord.
But that should also make us tremble.
Because if Jesus is present among His people, we cannot casually attach His name to our pride.
We cannot mistreat someone and assume that a religious title makes our actions righteous.
We cannot gather a few friends, agree to condemn somebody, and declare that heaven has endorsed our decision.
The presence of Christ is never permission to contradict the character of Christ.
Let that settle in your heart.
Jesus is not an accessory to our agenda.
He is Lord.
And His presence should make us more humble, more truthful, more merciful, and more careful with the lives entrusted to our care.
But perhaps you are wondering something.
Does this mean we should stop using Matthew 18:20 to encourage small prayer meetings?
Not necessarily.
We need to distinguish between what a verse primarily teaches and what may be a legitimate broader application.
Matthew 18:20 is not primarily a lesson about the minimum attendance required for Jesus to show up.
But that does not mean Christ abandons small gatherings.
The New Testament gives us abundant reasons to trust His presence with His people.
Jesus says in Matthew 28:20:
“Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.”
And in John 14:23, He speaks of the Father and Son making their dwelling with the one who loves Him and keeps His word.
The New Testament also teaches that the Holy Spirit dwells in believers.
So the presence of God is not activated by a second person entering the room.
Jesus is not absent from the faithful believer who prays alone.
Read that again.
Because someone needs it.
Maybe you have been praying by yourself for months.
Maybe the only sound in your bedroom at night is the ceiling fan and your own exhausted breathing.
Maybe you have nobody to pray with.
Nobody who knows how much you are struggling.
Nobody who understands why you have been crying over the same situation again and again.
And perhaps, somewhere in your mind, you have wondered whether your prayers are somehow less powerful because you are alone.
Listen carefully.
You do not need to find another person to make Jesus hear you.
The same Lord who taught His disciples to pray in secret in Matthew 6:6 has not forgotten the person who closes the bedroom door and whispers, “Father, help me.”
Your loneliness does not cancel His faithfulness.
Your tears are not disqualified because nobody else witnesses them.
Your prayers are not second-class prayers because there is only one voice speaking.
And your church is not spiritually inferior simply because it is small.
Two believers gathering faithfully to pray can be a beautiful expression of Christian fellowship.
So can two hundred.
The point is not that small prayer meetings are unbiblical.
The point is that Matthew 18:20 should not be reduced to a comforting slogan about attendance when Jesus gave it in a much more demanding context.
There is a difference between drawing encouragement from a biblical truth and replacing the original meaning of a passage with something easier to preach.
And the original meaning is not less beautiful.
It may actually be more beautiful.
Because it takes us into the places where Christians often struggle most.
The places where our faith becomes painfully practical.
Forgiveness.
Repentance.
Accountability.
Reconciliation.
And the question of whether we are willing to obey Jesus when obedience costs us something.
Think about the person whose name still makes your chest tighten.
The friend who betrayed your confidence.
The church member who spread something untrue about you.
The leader who disappointed you.
The family member who wounded you.
Or perhaps the person you hurt.
The one you have avoided because you do not want to face what you did.
The one whose forgiveness you want without having to admit the full truth.
The one you keep telling yourself should simply move on.
Jesus does not treat sin as a small thing.
But neither does He treat restoration as an insignificant thing.
And Matthew 18 does not end with verse 20.
That is where the next surprise comes.
Peter approaches Jesus and asks:
“Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?”
Jesus answers:
“I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.”
— Matthew 18:21–22, KJV
The expression translated “seventy times seven” is also understood by some interpreters as “seventy-seven times.” Either way, Jesus is not giving Peter a forgiveness calculator.
He is rejecting the idea that forgiveness should be limited to a convenient quota.
Then Jesus tells the parable of the unforgiving servant.
A servant owes his king an enormous debt.
A debt he cannot repay.
He pleads for mercy.
And the king forgives him.
But that same servant goes out and finds another servant who owes him a comparatively small amount.
Instead of extending mercy, he demands payment and has the man imprisoned.
The king hears what happened.
And the king is furious.
Why?
Because a man who had received extraordinary mercy refused to show mercy to someone else.
Do you see how Matthew 18 fits together?
The wandering sheep.
The brother who sins.
The private confrontation.
The witnesses.
The church.
The promise of Christ's presence.
Peter's question about forgiveness.
The unforgiving servant.
This is not a random collection of religious sayings.
It is a sustained lesson about life in the community of Jesus.
A community where sin must be taken seriously.
Where truth cannot be sacrificed.
Where people must not be discarded casually.
Where mercy is not optional.
Where forgiveness is rooted in the mercy we ourselves have received.
And where Christ remains the ultimate authority.
But we must say something important here.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending an offense never happened.
It does not mean restoring trust automatically.
It does not mean removing appropriate consequences.
It does not mean requiring a victim to remain in danger.
Forgiveness, reconciliation, restored trust, and renewed access are related but distinct matters.
A person can relinquish personal vengeance while still maintaining necessary boundaries and pursuing justice.
Repentance also matters.
And biblical repentance is more than saying, “I'm sorry you were offended.”
It is more than crying when consequences arrive.
It involves turning from sin, acknowledging wrong, and bearing fruit consistent with that change.
The Gospel never asks us to call evil good.
But it does call us to confront evil without abandoning the character of Christ.
And this is where the entire passage begins to lead us toward the cross.
Because before we were the people trying to correct somebody else…
We were sinners in need of mercy ourselves.
Before we could talk about restoring a brother…
We needed to be reconciled to God.
Before we could learn to forgive a debt…
We needed forgiveness for a debt we could never repay.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we made ourselves impressive.
Not after we cleaned up every secret.
Not after we became spiritually respectable.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And here is the scandal of grace.
The sinless Son of God entered a world of sinners.
He was rejected.
He was falsely accused.
He was condemned.
He was crucified.
And on that cross, He bore our sins, accomplishing what our religious efforts could never accomplish.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Not merely to make us feel better about ourselves.
But to save us from sin, reconcile us to God, and make us new.
Second Corinthians 5:18 says that God reconciled us to Himself by Jesus Christ.
That is the foundation.
We do not earn reconciliation with God by becoming exceptionally good at resolving human conflicts.
We are reconciled to God through Christ.
And because we have received His grace, we are called to become people who tell the truth, repent, forgive, and pursue peace.
Not perfectly.
Not without tears.
Not without difficult decisions.
But sincerely.
Because grace does not simply excuse the old life.
It begins to transform it.
Perhaps that is why this passage is so uncomfortable when we finally read it in context.
We would rather talk about Jesus being present at our prayer meetings than ask whether we have been obedient to Him in our relationships.
We would rather quote a promise than confront our pride.
We would rather discuss the power of agreement than admit how often we have participated in division.
We would rather say, “God is with us,” than ask whether the things we are doing truly honor Him.
And I am not writing this as someone who stands above that struggle.
These words confront every one of us.
Because all of us know how easy it is to defend ourselves.
How hard it is to apologize without excuses.
How tempting it is to expose somebody else's weakness while hiding our own.
How painful it is to forgive.
How frightening it can be to tell the truth.
And how desperately we need Jesus to change us.
Maybe this is the moment to stop asking only whether Christ is present in our gatherings…
…and begin asking whether we are willing to submit to Him when He speaks.
Are we willing to be corrected by Scripture?
Are we willing to repent when we are wrong?
Are we willing to pursue reconciliation where it is wise, safe, and possible?
Are we willing to protect the vulnerable?
Are we willing to stop using Bible verses as weapons for winning arguments?
Are we willing to love the truth more than our reputations?
Because the church does not become holy merely by saying the name of Jesus loudly.
The church is called to live under the Lordship of Jesus faithfully.
And sometimes, the clearest evidence of spiritual maturity is not the volume of our worship.
It is the humility of our repentance.
It is the courage to confess.
It is the willingness to correct without cruelty.
It is the patience to listen.
It is the mercy that refuses to become revenge.
It is the conviction that Christ's Word matters more than our comfort.
There is one more thing I want you to see.
Matthew 18:20 begins with the assurance that Jesus is among His gathered people.
But the Gospel does not end with Jesus standing at a distance, observing human conflict.
The Gospel brings us to the cross, where the One who had no sin gave Himself for sinners.
The Shepherd who spoke about the wandering sheep laid down His life for His sheep.
The Lord who taught His disciples about forgiveness became the sacrifice through whom forgiveness is offered.
The One who commands repentance also offers mercy to the repentant.
The One who teaches reconciliation is Himself the Mediator through whom sinners can come to the Father.
That is why the Christian faith is not simply a system of moral correction.
It is the announcement of a Savior.
A crucified and risen Savior.
And the deepest question in Matthew 18 is not merely whether two or three Christians are gathered.
It is whether we recognize the authority and grace of the Jesus in whose name we claim to gather.
Because you can sit in a crowded church and still resist His Word.
You can attend every prayer meeting and still refuse to repent.
You can memorize Matthew 18:20 and still ignore Matthew 18:15.
You can speak beautifully about forgiveness while holding tightly to bitterness.
And you can be surrounded by religious people while desperately needing to surrender your heart to Christ.
But there is good news.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing something in you right now, you do not need to run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn from what needs to be abandoned.
Seek forgiveness where you have done wrong.
Pursue wise and truthful restoration where possible.
And where you have been deeply wounded, bring that wound before the Lord without believing that healing requires you to deny what happened.
Jesus does not demand that you pretend.
He calls you into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is mercy for the repentant.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is hope for the person who has wandered.
There is forgiveness through the blood of Jesus Christ.
And there is a new way to live.
Not because we are strong enough to rewrite our own stories.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
That is not merely a beautiful phrase.
It is the testimony of the Gospel.
Peter denied Jesus, yet the risen Christ restored him and entrusted him with responsibility.
Paul persecuted the church, yet the grace of God transformed him into a witness of the very Gospel he once opposed.
And the thief crucified beside Jesus had no opportunity to build an impressive religious record, yet he turned to Christ in faith and received the promise of paradise.
Different lives.
Different failures.
The same extraordinary Savior.
No, grace does not make sin harmless.
Grace reveals how serious sin is, because the forgiveness of sinners came at the cost of the cross.
And grace reveals how astonishing God's mercy is, because the crucified Christ rose again.
So the next time someone quotes Matthew 18:20 at a small prayer meeting, you do not need to embarrass them.
You do not need to turn a sincere moment of encouragement into a theological competition.
You can rejoice that Jesus is faithful to His people.
And perhaps, when the moment is right, you can gently explain that the verse has an even richer context.
It reminds us that the Lord is among His people as they submit to His authority, seek truth, confront sin responsibly, and pursue the restoration He commands.
And maybe that conversation will lead someone to read Matthew 18 for themselves.
Maybe it will help a wounded believer understand that biblical accountability should never be an excuse for spiritual abuse.
Maybe it will encourage a church leader to handle a difficult matter with greater humility.
Maybe it will move someone to apologize.
Maybe it will help someone stop weaponizing Scripture.
Maybe it will remind a lonely Christian that the presence of Jesus is not dependent on the number of chairs occupied in a room.
And maybe…
Just maybe…
It will bring someone back to the Savior they have been avoiding.
If this message exposed an area where pride, resentment, fear, or hidden sin has been standing between you and obedience to Christ, you do not have to describe your private situation publicly.
You do not need to reveal names or painful details.
Sometimes those three words are enough to remind another believer that someone needs compassion, not judgment.
Not to glorify the failure.
But to glorify the Savior who met you in it.
There may be someone reading who believes their past has permanently disqualified them from being loved by God.
Your testimony might help them hear the Gospel with fresh hope.
Not because every sentence I have written is beyond correction, but because the Scriptures we have examined deserve to be studied carefully.
Return to Matthew 18.
Read the entire chapter.
Examine the context.
Compare Scripture with Scripture.
Let the Word of God correct anything that needs correcting, including anything you read here.

And if someone comes to mind who has been struggling with church hurt, forgiveness, spiritual isolation, or confusion about this passage, consider tagging them gently or sending this article privately.
Not everyone who needs this message will ever walk into a church building this week.
Some are scrolling through Facebook with questions they are afraid to ask.
Some have walked away from Christian fellowship because of how they were treated.
Some are searching for the truth about Jesus beneath years of religious disappointment.
And some are one honest conversation away from opening their Bible again.
A thoughtful share can help put Scripture in front of someone who needs it.
That is one of the reasons Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish inspirational words that disappear after a few seconds of scrolling.
But to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ, the authority of Scripture, the necessity of repentance, the beauty of grace, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
And invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still exploring Christianity to follow along.
There is room here for sincere questions.
There is room for people who are learning.
There is room for those who are seeking healing.
And there must always be room for the truth of Scripture to challenge all of us.
These resources are part of our commitment to making biblical learning and Christian encouragement more accessible.
It does not purchase His favor.
It does not make you a more valuable Christian.
And it is not a replacement for your responsibility to give faithfully and wisely according to biblical conviction, including your responsibilities toward your local church and those in need.
But it can be a voluntary, recurring expression of generosity toward Gospel-centered ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which I want to extend this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
The greater purpose is the work itself.
More biblical truth made accessible.
More believers encouraged to study the Word.
More people pointed toward repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and faith in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The invitation to repent and believe in Jesus Christ is not behind a paywall.
The grace of God cannot be purchased.
Your worth before God is not measured by your financial contribution.
If you cannot give, you can still pray.
You can still encourage someone.
You can still study Scripture and grow in Christ.
And you can still help spread the truth that Jesus saves sinners.
It must always lead beyond us.
Back to the Bible.
Back to the cross.
Back to the empty tomb.
Back to Jesus.
A small prayer meeting.
A few empty chairs.
A familiar verse.
“Where two or three are gathered…”
We thought it was mainly about the number of people who showed up.
But Jesus was teaching something that reaches much deeper.
He was teaching His disciples how to live as a community under His authority.
How to confront sin.
How to protect truth.
How to seek restoration.
How to forgive.
How to remember that the church belongs to Him.
And perhaps the next time you hear those words, you will remember that Christ's presence is not an excuse to avoid the difficult things He commands.
It is the reason we can face them with humility, courage, and hope.
So if there is sin to confess, do not keep hiding.
If there is a wrong to make right, do not let pride become your prison.
If there is a wound that needs healing, bring it honestly to the Lord.
If there is a passage you have misunderstood, do not be ashamed to learn.
And if you have been measuring God's nearness by how many people stand beside you, remember the Savior who promised to remain with His disciples.
Your faith does not rest on a crowd.
It rests on Christ.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls His people into truth.
The One whose mercy is greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
And the One who is still able to transform lives that seem hopelessly broken.
Because the greatest tragedy is not discovering that you misunderstood a Bible verse—it is hearing the voice of Jesus in His Word and refusing to let Him change your heart.
